title: Capstone 2: a persistent priority queue
body: A leftist heap is a persistent priority queue. It is a binary tree where every node is no larger than its children (the heap property) and the *rank*, the length of the right spine, of the left child is at least that of the right child. That second rule keeps the right spine short, which is what makes `merge` logarithmic.

Everything is built on `merge`. To merge two heaps, compare their roots, keep the smaller root, and recursively merge the *right* subtree of that heap with the other heap; then swap children if needed so the rank rule holds. `insert` merges a one-node heap in, and `delete_min` merges the root's two children. One recursive function gives the whole API.

Because nodes are immutable and shared, an old heap remains valid after any operation, which is persistence. The `Make` functor takes the element ordering as a module argument, the same shape as `Map.Make`, so the heap works for ints, strings or your own record type without polymorphic comparison.
challenge: In src/leftist.ml, `merge` returns its first argument, so inserting loses elements. Implement it: if either heap is empty return the other; otherwise keep the smaller root `x`, merge the right subtree with the other heap, and rebuild the node with `make` (which restores the rank rule).
projectInstructions: Run `dune test --root .`. Edit only `merge` in src/leftist.ml. The test compares against List.sort on random inputs and checks that old heaps are unchanged.
question: Why is an old leftist heap still valid after `delete_min`?
correct: Operations build new nodes and share the unchanged subtrees, so the original structure is never mutated
wrong: delete_min copies the whole heap first
The old heap is deleted but its elements remain in a hidden array
reasoning: Persistent structures never overwrite nodes; updates allocate new nodes along the changed path and reuse everything else.
